drainage.local_h: Where Tyler's water comes from, and where it should go
local: Tyler drainage follows the rules of the rest of East Texas. Sandy loam sits on top, red clay lies underneath, and once the top foot is full the water moves sideways. It can end up at your foundation, in a back corner or at the bottom of a slope. Walking the lot during or right after a rain is the best way to see it, and we do that when we can.

Newer Tyler subdivisions have a typical story. The house sits on a graded pad, the lot settles after construction and a flat backyard starts holding water. Often the cure is regrading, a swale and a pop-up emitter, well short of a French drain. Older neighborhoods have the opposite story, decades of settled grade and downspouts that dump into flat beds beside the house. We look at the downspouts first, since roof water is the most common source.

Slope matters in Tyler. Where a lot drops toward the street or the back fence, water speeds up, washes out beds and undercuts walkways. We handle erosion control and the drainage behind retaining walls as well. If you have azaleas or roses in those beds, they will not tolerate wet feet for long, so fixing the water protects the plants too. The walk shows us where the water is heading before we propose any digging.

When a French drain is the answer, we dig a trench with a steady fall to a real outlet: daylight, a curb, a lower part of the lot or a pop-up emitter. Sock-wrapped pipe goes in with #57 stone so clay fines cannot clog it. A standard single run is $1,900 to $3,000, full systems run $3,000 to $4,500, and large combined projects run $4,500 and up. We finish the trench in sod or river rock.

faq.q: What does drainage work cost in Tyler?

faq.q: Why does water pool against my foundation?
faq.a: Usually roof water dumped into a flat bed, ground that settled toward the house, or water stopping on the clay layer and spreading sideways. Each has a different fix. We find the real cause before pricing anything, ideally during or right after rain.

faq.q: Do I need a French drain, or is there a cheaper fix?
faq.a: Often there is a cheaper fix. Downspout extensions, regrading, a swale or a pop-up emitter solve many wet yards. We recommend a French drain only when the water source needs one, and the written estimate says what we install and why.

faq.q: Why do some French drains stop working?
faq.a: Cheap ones use corrugated pipe in a rock bag, laid shallow with no real outlet, and clay fines clog them in a season or two. We use sock-wrapped pipe and #57 stone with a steady fall to a place the water can actually leave.

fertilization.local_h: Feeding Tyler lawns on the grass's calendar, not the store's
local: Soil testing matters more in Tyler than most places because of the azaleas. Older neighborhoods like the Azalea District put acid-loving shrubs in beds right beside the turf. East Texas soil already runs a little low on pH, and lime is the cure for that, but lime is not something to spread near azaleas by habit. We pull a sample, read the numbers and add lime only where the lawn needs it.

The calendar is set by soil temperature. The first feeding goes down around April 25, once nights hold above 60 and the grass is fully awake. Feed in March and most of it rinses out with the next rain, because bermuda and St. Augustine cannot pull it in yet. The last real nitrogen lands in the first two weeks of September, well ahead of the first freeze. Waiting for the soil, not the calendar page, is what keeps the money in the lawn.

October is a potassium month. Plenty of Tyler lawns are St. Augustine under oaks, and that grass is the one large patch likes to attack when nights drop into the 60s and the blades stay damp. A heavy nitrogen shot then feeds the fungus. The winterizer is built around potassium for cold hardiness instead, and that is why the store's fall bag is the wrong fit. Bermuda lawns in sunny yards get their own plan, with the same four visits.

Newer Tyler subdivisions bring a different issue. Builders grade with compacted fill, and rain runs off it instead of soaking in. Those lawns are good candidates for core aeration between late August and mid-September, with the September feeding right behind it. Bigger lots out toward Whitehouse and Chapel Hill price by lawn size and by how many rounds the soil test calls for. Zoysia lawns follow a plan of their own, and you see it in writing before the first application.

flower-bed-installation.local_h: Roses, azaleas and the light your bed really gets

Roses want six or more hours of it and enough room for air to move through, so we site them in full sun and space them wider than the nursery tag suggests. Shade is the other Tyler bed. Under the pines and oaks that cover older lots, azaleas and hydrangeas are the better fit, and they want afternoon shade. We plant for the light the bed gets, not whatever looked good on the rack that week. Walk the spot at 4 p.m. in July and tell us what you see. That tells us more than the plant list does. Hydrangeas in particular want that afternoon relief.

The ground matters as much as the plants. Newer Tyler subdivisions often have beds built on compacted fill under thin mulch. We loosen the soil and work compost into the clay, cut a clean edge in stone, steel or natural cut, and plant with spacing so the air moves through. Then mulch goes down at an inch to an inch and a half, pulled back off the stems. Pulling weeds by the root at this stage saves you a summer of them.

Timing helps. Perennials and shrubs do best planted from September through November, while the soil is warm. Heat lovers like vinca wait until mid-May, since a cool, wet spring rots them. After install we walk you through watering: deep and less often, so roots go down. If you want to see the layout first, the $199 Flower Bed Preview gives you a rendering. Watering deep and less often keeps roots from rotting in wet clay.

Newer subdivisions have the opposite problem. Builders plant shrubs tight to the foundation, and after a few seasons they are against the siding, over the windows and rubbing the brick. The calendar changes by plant. Hollies and boxwoods take their main shaping in June, after the spring flush, so the new growth hardens before cold weather. Azaleas in Tyler beds get cut right after the bloom and no later, because they set next year's buds in summer. A hard shearing in late fall is the one cut we skip, since the tender regrowth burns brown with the first freeze. That timing is why a hedge cut in the wrong month can look worse than one left alone.

Cleanup is part of the price. Tarps go down first, every clipping is raked up and blown out of the beds, and we haul all of it away, so you are not left with piles by the curb. Most Tyler hedges want two to three trims between spring and fall. We can set you up on a recurring schedule or come back when you call. Ligustrum, photinia and Japanese yew get the same care.

mulch-installation.title: Mulch Installation in Tyler, TX: Beds Done Right | Yard Dog

mulch-installation.h1: Mulch for Tyler beds, laid at the depth that works
mulch-installation.lede: Clean edges, weeds pulled by the root and an even layer of mulch, kept off the stems of azaleas, hollies and tree trunks.
mulch-installation.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes, a family-owned and fully insured company based in Longview, installs mulch in Tyler. mulch-installation.local_h: A mulch refresh that finishes the whole Tyler yard
local: A mulch job pairs well with other work in Tyler. If the hedges need a trim or the beds need a cleanup, doing it on the same trip means the whole yard gets finished at once, which makes sense at this distance. We edge, pull out the old buildup and put fresh mulch down over beds that are clean, not over last year's weeds and leaves. Tell us about the hedges when you ask, and we will price it together.

Depth is where most Tyler beds go wrong. An online calculator will say three inches, but that is a northern number for snow country. Here, three inches sheds light rain, holds moisture against stems until they rot and gives voles cover to eat roots. We lay an inch to an inch and a half. On a 2,000 square foot bed that is about 8 yards, not 19. The right depth also saves you money on material.

Azaleas and roses care most. Azalea roots are shallow, and mulch piled against the stems is how a good plant gets lost. We taper it off at every stem and trunk. Under the pines on older lots, pine straw is a fine pick, and shredded hardwood is the usual choice for roses. On newer lots with compacted fill, we loosen the crusted top inch first so rain reaches the roots.

Fabric stays out of mulched beds. Mulch turns into soil, and fabric under it ends up with weeds rooted on top and through it. Fabric does belong under rock, and we use it there. The best windows are late April through mid-May and late September through October, when a thin top-dress goes down before the leaves and the first cold front. We also haul away the debris and blow off the walks and drive before we leave.

faq.q: How much does mulch cost in Tyler?
faq.a: Most bed refreshes run $600 to $2,400, depending on square footage, number of beds, mulch type, edging and weed pulling, and whether it is a full install or a thin top-dress. A fall top-dress over a layer that is still there often costs a fraction of a full install.

faq.q: How deep should mulch be?
faq.a: An inch to an inch and a half, raked even and pulled back from stems and trunks. Three inches is a northern habit that causes trouble here: it sheds light rain, traps moisture against stems and shelters voles. Keep that in mind when you compare quotes.

faq.q: Which mulch should go around my azaleas?
faq.a: Pine straw or shredded hardwood both work, laid thin and kept off the stems. Azalea roots are shallow, so we avoid piling anything deep. We also offer cypress, cedar and dyed black or brown, and we will help you choose.

faq.q: Do you put weed fabric under mulch in Tyler?
faq.a: No. Within a few years it has weeds growing on top and through it, and it keeps mulch from turning into soil. We pull weeds by the root and edge the bed instead. Fabric does go under rock beds, and we use it there.

faq.q: When should Tyler beds be mulched?
faq.a: Late April through mid-May is the main window, right after spring growth and before the heat. A thin top-dress in late September through October is the second. Either can be combined with a hedge trim or bed cleanup on one visit.

retaining-walls.title: Retaining Walls in Tyler, TX: Block, Stone, Timber | Yard Dog
retaining-walls.meta: Retaining walls in Tyler, TX for sloping lots: block and stone on a compacted base with a drain behind. Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000 by height and length.
retaining-walls.h1: Retaining walls that turn Tyler slopes into usable yard
retaining-walls.lede: Segmental block and natural stone walls for Tyler lots that fall toward the street or the back fence, built on a real base with drainage behind them.
retaining-walls.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes, a family-owned and fully insured company based in Longview, builds retaining walls in Tyler. We use segmental block or natural stone on a compacted base set below grade, with gravel backfill and a drain to daylight behind it. Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000, set mostly by height and length. We are rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews, and a wall is a one-time project, so Tyler's distance is no problem.
retaining-walls.local_h: Holding back a slope on a Tyler lot
local: Where a Tyler lot drops toward the street or the back fence, rain does damage. It washes out beds, undercuts walkways and leaves a slope nobody can use. A wall there earns its cost by turning that slope into level yard. We walk the site, measure the grade change, find where the water comes from and work out what the wall has to hold back. That walk tells us whether a wall, a terrace or just better grading is the right answer.

Water is why walls fail in this part of the state. Sandy loam over red clay swells when wet and shrinks when dry, and behind a wall that water has nowhere to go. Pressure builds until the wall leans, then bows, then cracks. So every wall we build gets a gravel chimney and a perforated drain pipe at the bottom, run out to daylight so the water has a place to go.

The second weak spot is the base. We excavate below grade, compact crushed stone and set the first course dead level, because everything above it follows. Taller walls get geogrid tied into the backfill. A very steep grade can be broken into terraces, which are often easier to build well than a single tall wall. A leaning wall can be rebuilt course by course. Wet clay will not pack down right, so we dig and compact in a dry stretch.

Height changes the job. Walls over about four feet usually need engineered design and reinforcement. We handle the base prep, geogrid and drainage those walls need, and if the project calls for a stamped engineering plan, we tell you at the walkthrough, before anyone digs. Short garden walls start at a few thousand dollars, and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up. We also grade the ground above and below the wall so water moves off.

faq.q: What does a retaining wall cost in Tyler?
faq.a: Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000. Height and length drive the number, along with material, excavation, drainage and geogrid on taller walls. Short garden walls start at a few thousand dollars and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up. The walkthrough is free.

faq.q: Does a taller wall need an engineer?
faq.a: Walls over about four feet usually need engineered design and reinforcement. We do the base, geogrid and drainage work, and if your wall needs a stamped engineering plan, we tell you during the walkthrough so there are no surprises. The estimate is itemized.

faq.q: Why does every wall need drainage?
faq.a: Because East Texas clay holds water and swells, and water pressing on a wall is what makes it lean. We put gravel backfill behind it and a perforated pipe at the base, with an outlet where the water can leave. Every wall gets one.

faq.q: Can a leaning wall be fixed?
faq.a: Often by rebuilding it. We take it down, redo the base, and rebuild course by course with proper backfill and a drain behind it. If the cause was water, adding drainage is the real fix, not just stacking the same blocks back.

faq.q: What material is best for a wall on a sloped lot?
faq.a: Segmental block, natural stone, boulder and timber all work. Block suits taller or engineered walls, stone suits the look of older homes, and timber suits low garden walls. We price each on the walkthrough and tell you which holds up best.

sod-installation.local_h: Picking the grass by sun, not by price, across Tyler
local: Sod suits Tyler because it is one job with a start and a finish. We make the trip, do the prep and lay it, and then the work is done. The first decision is the grass. Walk your yard in July and note where the sun really lands. That decides it, more than cost does, and we help you map it before we quote. Tell us which parts of the yard bake and which stay shaded, and we will recommend a grass, or a split, for each area.

Open yards in newer subdivisions and on larger lots toward Lake Tyler and Whitehouse are bermuda ground. We usually lay Tif419 in full sun. The shaded yards under older oaks and pines are a different story. Bermuda quits in shade and thins to dirt by August no matter what you feed it. There we lay St. Augustine, in Floratam, Palmetto or Raleigh depending on how much shade the spot demands.

Be honest about the deep shade too. Under about four hours of sun no turf thrives long term, and some Azalea District yards have spots like that under mature canopy. Those spots are better as a shade bed or a mulched area, and we say so rather than sell you sod that will not last. Compacted builder fill is the other common problem, and tilling in two to three inches of compost fixes it.

Timing is simple. Bermuda goes down from late April through August and St. Augustine from May through September, and St. Augustine needs four to six weeks of root growth before dormancy. Then comes the part that decides whether the money was well spent. Plan on a deep morning watering every day for two weeks, then taper. We write the schedule down with you before install day. If you skip the watering, a $4,000 install can brown out in two weeks.

faq.q: How much does sod cost in Tyler?
faq.a: Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700. Sod is priced by the pallet, so square footage drives the number. Grass type, old turf removal, grading, soil amendment, drainage and access for pallets all play in. You get a written quote after we measure.

faq.q: Which grass should I choose for my Tyler yard?
faq.a: Sun decides it. Full sun gets bermuda, usually Tif419. Shade under oaks and pines gets St. Augustine in a variety matched to the shade. Under about four hours of sun, no turf holds up, and we will tell you if a spot is better left as a bed.

faq.q: When is the best time to lay sod?
faq.a: Bermuda from late April through August, and St. Augustine from May through September. Get St. Augustine down by the end of September so it has four to six weeks of rooting before dormancy. Sod laid in November just sits on the ground.

faq.q: Do you prep the ground first?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the part that matters most. Old turf and weeds come out, the grade is set, and two to three inches of compost or topsoil is tilled in, leveled and rolled. Then the sod goes down with starter fertilizer underneath.

faq.q: Can you patch dead spots instead of replacing the whole lawn?
faq.a: Yes. We do patch repairs and plugs as well as full-yard installs. A small repair costs less than a full job. If the patch is dead because of shade or drainage, we tell you, since new sod would fail there the same way.

tree-planting.title: Tree Planting in Tyler, TX: Dogwoods, Oaks & More | Yard Dog
tree-planting.meta: Tree planting in Tyler, TX: dogwood, redbud, live oak, post oak and magnolia set at the right depth with a watering plan. Quoted after a free walkthrough.
tree-planting.h1: Planting the right tree for your Tyler yard
tree-planting.lede: Dogwoods, redbuds and long-lived shade trees planted at the right depth, with a mulch ring and a written watering plan for the first year.
tree-planting.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes, a family-owned and fully insured company based in Longview, plants trees in Tyler. We match the species to your soil, sun and space, dig wide and shallow, set the root flare at grade and leave a mulch ring and a written watering plan. The tree drives most of the cost, so we quote after a free walkthrough. We are rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
tree-planting.local_h: Dappled light, red clay and a six-month head start
local: Spring in Tyler leans on dogwoods and redbuds, and both want what the edge of a bigger tree gives them: dappled light, not a full afternoon of sun. That makes placement the first job. In the Azalea District, where mature canopy already covers the lot, we look for the spot a dogwood will actually thrive, then check how far it sits from the house, the drive and the neighbor's fence line.

For long-lived shade, the usual Tyler picks are live oak, post oak and southern magnolia. Those need room, so we think about the tree at forty years, not at planting. Bigger lots out past Loop 323, around Whitehouse and Chapel Hill, can hold a live oak well away from the foundation. A tight lot in a newer subdivision may do better with a smaller tree set where it will not crowd the roof.

Newer subdivisions come with young trees and compacted fill. A hole dug into packed builder soil acts like a bowl and holds water. So we dig wide and shallow, cut any circling roots, set the root flare at grade and backfill with native soil, with no pocket of bagged mix. We would often rather plant a smaller tree that roots in fast than a big one that sulks for three years.

Fall is the planting window, from October through February when the weather allows. A tree set in October gets about six months of root growth before summer, while an April tree gets about eight weeks. After planting you get a written watering schedule, and on bigger installs we come back around the 30-day mark to check how the tree is establishing. We build a watering basin, lay a mulch ring off the trunk and stake only when the wind calls for it. Stock comes from regional growers, and we pick it ourselves.

faq.q: What do you charge to plant a tree in Tyler?
faq.a: We do not publish a price, because the tree is most of the cost. Species, size at planting, number of trees, access and soil all matter. After a free walkthrough you get a written quote that includes the aftercare plan.

faq.q: Where should I put a dogwood or redbud?
faq.a: At the edge of bigger trees, where it gets dappled light and some afternoon relief. Full all-day sun in July is harder on them. We check the spot's light, drainage and distance from structures before we recommend a species or a location.

faq.q: Which shade tree is best for a bigger Tyler lot?
faq.a: Live oak, post oak and southern magnolia are the usual long-lived choices. Which one fits depends on the room, the soil and what you want it to do. We recommend after seeing the lot, and we plan around the full-grown size.

faq.q: Why plant in fall instead of spring?
faq.a: The soil stays warm for weeks after the air cools. A tree planted in October builds roots through the winter and meets summer with six months behind it. A spring tree can work, but it needs steady watering on the root ball all through its first summer.

faq.q: How do I water a new tree?
faq.a: Soak the root ball itself, with a hose on a trickle for about twenty minutes. A fall tree needs that twice a week for six weeks, then weekly through November. Soak everything new the day before a hard freeze. We write the schedule out for your tree.

tree-shrub-care.title: Tree & Shrub Care in Tyler, TX: Pruning by Season | Yard Dog
tree-shrub-care.meta: Tree and shrub care in Tyler, TX: azaleas cut after bloom, crepe myrtles thinned not topped, small tree removal and full haul-off. Quoted after a free walkthrough.
tree-shrub-care.h1: Pruning Tyler's azaleas, crepe myrtles and oaks in their own seasons
tree-shrub-care.lede: In Tyler's older neighborhoods the shrubs are the landscape, so timing every cut matters. We prune each plant in its window and haul off every limb.
tree-shrub-care.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes, a family-owned and fully insured company based in Longview, handles tree and shrub care in Tyler. We prune and shape on each plant's schedule, thin crepe myrtles instead of topping them, remove small trees and shrubs, and haul off all the cuttings. No two yards have the same plants, so we quote after a free walkthrough. We are rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
tree-shrub-care.local_h: Why the calendar decides every cut in a Tyler yard
local: Azaleas and dogwoods in the Azalea District have decades of growth on them, and the wrong cut at the wrong time costs a whole season of bloom. Azaleas and camellias get pruned right after they flower, never sheared in fall. On a leggy, overgrown azalea we cut back the longest stems and thin the dead wood, and a very overgrown plant may get a harder cut spread over two seasons.

Roses are a Tyler tradition, and Knockout roses get cut back hard in February, along with the crepe myrtles. Crepe myrtles are thinned while dormant and before the buds break. We do not top them. Topping makes a crepe myrtle regrow taller on weaker wood, and a tree that is wrong for its spot needs a smaller variety, not a saw. If yours has been topped, recovery takes two or three winters.

Oaks are on a different clock, and East Texas has oak wilt. Beetles drawn to fresh pruning cuts help carry it, and they are most active in spring and early summer. So healthy oaks wait until the cold months. When a storm breaks a limb, we cut it clean and seal the wound with pruning sealer right away. We do not take down large trees near structures, and we say so up front.

Hollies and boxwoods get shaped in early summer. Beyond pruning, the service covers dead lower limbs on shade trees, seasonal feeding for trees and shrubs, a mulch refresh around tree bases, small tree and shrub removal, and storm cleanup. Every limb, trimming and handful of sawdust is raked up and hauled away before we leave. Dead lower limbs come off shade trees so the lawn can be mowed under them again. Hollies, yaupons and other shrubs along the foundation are shaped the same way, one plant at a time, and a quote after the walkthrough lists each job separately.

faq.q: When should I prune my azaleas in Tyler?
faq.a: Right after they finish blooming in spring, and no later than mid-June. They set next year's flower buds over the summer, so a cut in July or fall removes the blooms. We do not shear azaleas in fall. Cutting much past mid-June costs you flowers.

faq.q: Can you bring back a leggy, overgrown azalea?
faq.a: Usually. We remove dead wood and cut back the longest stems right after bloom. A badly overgrown plant may need a harder cut spread over two seasons so it does not go into shock. We tell you what to expect before we cut.

faq.q: Why do you wait to prune oaks?
faq.a: Oak wilt. The beetles that help spread the fungus are drawn to fresh sap from pruning cuts, and they are most active in spring and early summer. We prune healthy oaks in the cold months and clean up storm-broken limbs right away.

faq.q: Do you remove trees and stumps in Tyler?
faq.a: We remove small trees and shrubs. We do not remove large trees near structures, and we do not grind stumps. If a job is beyond our scope, we say so at the walkthrough instead of taking it on and doing it badly.

faq.q: How do I get a price for tree and shrub care?
faq.a: Ask for a free walkthrough. We identify each tree and shrub, flag what needs work and what to leave alone, and send an itemized quote, usually within a day. Count, size, condition and access all affect the price, so we do not publish a flat number.
